90901.text: What does the term "air traffic" cover?
options: All aircraft in flight or operating on the manoeuvring area of an aerodrome
All vehicles on the apron and parking area
Only aircraft with an IFR flight plan

90902.text: When an air traffic control clearance is abbreviated to "clearance", which words may precede it to indicate the portion of flight it relates to?
options: Taxi, take-off, en-route, approach or landing

90903.text: What is the purpose of the air traffic control service?
options: To prevent collisions between aircraft and to maintain and expedite an orderly flow of traffic on the manoeuvring area
To prepare flight plans for pilots

90904.text: How is Runway Visual Range (RVR) defined?
options: The range over which the pilot of an aircraft on the runway centre line can see the runway markings, the lights delineating the runway or the centre line
The distance from which the tower controller can see the runway end
The distance at which the aircraft on the approach first sees the aerodrome
The horizontal visibility measured at the meteorological station
The maximum distance at which runway lights are visible at night
Continuous service throughout day and night
The magnetic heading to fly to a station
The true bearing from the station to the aircraft
The aircraft's distance from the station
Height above the aerodrome reference point
The altimeter setting referenced to sea level

90908.text: With wind present, how is the heading to fly obtained from QDM?
options: By applying a wind correction angle to the QDM
By flying the QDM as it is
By taking the reciprocal of the QDM
By adding magnetic variation to the QDM
By using QNH instead of QDM

90909.text: What are messages stating that an aircraft is in serious or imminent danger called?

90910.text: Into which category do messages concerning the safety of an aircraft, another vehicle or a person on board fall?

90911.text: From which frequency does an airborne pilot usually request aerodrome weather information?

90912.text: If the weather information given also covers the runway in use, what does the pilot read back together with the QNH?

90913.text: At aerodromes where no suitable dedicated ATIS frequency is available, where may ATIS be broadcast?
options: On the voice channel of the aerodrome VOR identification

90914.text: If the current ATIS broadcast is "INFORMATION ALPHA", how is the updated new broadcast identified?

90915.text: Which of the following is NOT part of an ATIS broadcast?
options: Runway in use and wind information

90916.text: What is the basic difference between ATIS and VOLMET?
options: ATIS gives information for a single aerodrome, while VOLMET covers several aerodromes in the area
ATIS is broadcast on HF, VOLMET only on VHF
VOLMET gives only runway state, ATIS only weather
ATIS is requested by the pilot, VOLMET is broadcast continuously

90917.text: What does "NOSIG" in a VOLMET broadcast mean?
options: No significant weather change is expected within 2 hours
The broadcast is no longer valid

90918.text: On which frequency bands are VOLMET broadcasts made?

90919.text: What is the cloud condition included in CAVOK?
options: No cloud below 5000 ft or below MSA
No cloud at all in the sky

90920.text: Which of the following is NOT a condition of CAVOK?
options: No cloud below 5000 ft or MSA

90921.text: For which three points along the runway is RVR assessed?
options: Touchdown zone, midpoint and stop end
Runway threshold, runway centre and apron
Initial approach fix, decision altitude and threshold

90922.text: Which of the following is correct about transmitting RVR information by radio?
options: It is given in metres, is not spoken using the phonetic alphabet and does not need to be read back
It is given in feet and must always be read back
It is spelled out using the phonetic alphabet
It is given in kilometres only
Every digit must be repeated phonetically

90923.text: Why is a dry or damp runway usually not stated in runway surface condition reports?
options: Unless otherwise stated, the runway is understood to be dry or damp
This information is given only by NOTAM
Dry and damp runways do not affect performance
This information is given only at night
This information is included in the flight plan

90924.text: If the runway surface is covered with snow or ice, what additional report is given to the pilot?
options: A braking action report; the runway friction coefficient is categorised from low to high
The status of the approach lights

90925.text: How is the number 53 148 spoken in radiotelephony?
options: Fifty-three thousand one hundred and forty-eight
Five, three thousand, one hundred and forty-eight

90926.text: When transmitting time in aviation, what is spoken if there is no possibility of confusion?

90927.text: To which reference is time expressed in aviation?
options: UTC on the 24-hour clock (also called GMT or Zulu)
Local time of the departure aerodrome
Local time of the destination aerodrome
Any time zone chosen by the pilot

90928.text: What should be done before transmitting after changing frequency?
options: Listen on the frequency for about 5 seconds to make sure no other transmission will be interrupted
First listen on the emergency frequency

90929.text: What is the correct speaking rate in radio communication?

90930.text: What is the most common error in using the transmit button?
options: Releasing the button before finishing the message
Pressing the button before starting to speak
Releasing the button after the message is finished

90931.text: What happens if the microphone is too far from the lips?
options: The voice level weakens and the microphone also picks up other cockpit noise, making the message hard to understand
The voice is distorted and the message becomes unintelligible

90932.text: What happens if the microphone is too close to the lips?
options: The voice is distorted and the message becomes unintelligible
Cockpit noise mixes into the message

90933.text: What is the purpose of leaving occasional pauses in a long radio message?
options: To check whether the frequency is still clear and whether any part of the message needs repeating
To let the transmit button cool down
To let the controller record the message

90934.text: Which call signs are used on initial contact with an aeronautical ground station?
options: The full call signs of both the aeronautical ground station and the aircraft
Only the aircraft's abbreviated call sign
Only the name of the ground station
The last two letters of the aircraft registration

90935.text: When may abbreviated call signs be used?
options: Only after the ground station has decided no confusion will arise and has used the abbreviation first
Whenever the pilot considers it appropriate
At the pilot's discretion when the frequency is busy

90936.text: How is the call sign of an aeronautical ground station formed?
options: The name of the station followed by a suffix indicating the type of service provided
Only the ICAO code of the aerodrome
The controller's first and last name
The frequency number and the aerodrome name
The country code and the aerodrome name

90937.text: How is a Type 1 aircraft call sign (the ICAO registration marking) abbreviated?
options: The first character of the registration followed by its last two characters
The last three characters of the registration
The first two characters of the registration

90938.text: How is a Type 3 call sign (the operator's radiotelephony designator followed by the flight number) abbreviated?
options: There is no abbreviated form for this type of call sign
Only the flight number is spoken
Only the operator designator is spoken
The last two digits of the flight number are spoken
The operator designator and the first digit of the flight number are spoken

90939.text: What does a Type 2 call sign consist of?
options: The operator's radiotelephony designator followed by the last four characters of the ICAO registration marking
The operator's radiotelephony designator and the flight number
The aircraft type and the registration marking
The aerodrome name and the flight number

90940.text: What must an aircraft under air traffic control do if it wishes to change frequency on its own initiative?
options: First obtain permission from the relevant air traffic control unit
Make a blind transmission and change frequency
Switch directly to the new frequency and call

90941.text: In what order is a pilot's radio check call made?
options: Call sign of the station called, aircraft call sign, the words "Radio check", the frequency in use
Aircraft call sign, frequency in use, station called, "Radio check"
"Radio check", frequency in use, aircraft call sign
Frequency in use, station called, "Radio check"
Aircraft call sign and "Radio check" are sufficient

90942.text: What information should a ground station give when replying to a radio check call?
options: The call sign of the aircraft requesting the check, the call sign of the replying station, and the readability of the call
Only its own call sign and frequency
Aerodrome weather and runway in use
The aircraft call sign and the QNH

90943.text: Which of the following is NOT among the items the pilot must read back verbatim?

90944.text: What else does the pilot's verbatim read-back of a clearance confirm to the controller?
options: That the clearance was given to the correct aircraft and that only that aircraft will act on it
That the pilot has set the frequency correctly
That the aircraft transponder is operating
That the pilot has the ATIS information
That the aircraft has sufficient fuel
I have received all of your last transmission
I understand the instruction and will comply

90946.text: Which of the following is an example of a communication problem caused by human error?
options: The receiver volume turned down too low or the wrong frequency selected
Power failure at the ground station

90947.text: In the physical checks made when radio failure is suspected, what is checked regarding the squelch?
options: That the squelch level is not set higher than necessary
That the squelch is fully closed
That the squelch is at the highest level
That the squelch is set to the emergency frequency
That the squelch matches the transponder

90948.text: How is signal range calculated from the aircraft's height in feet?
options: The square root of the height multiplied by 1.25
The square root of the height multiplied by 12

90949.text: How is signal range approximately found from the flight level?
options: By multiplying the square root of the flight level by 12
By multiplying the flight level by 12
By multiplying the square root of the flight level by 1.25
By multiplying the flight level by 100
By dividing the flight level by two

90950.text: If two-way communication with the ground station cannot be established after the physical checks, what is tried first?
options: Contacting on the frequency of another air traffic control unit such as Tower, Approach or Ground
Communicating with other aircraft on the route
Making a MAYDAY call on 121.5 MHz

90951.text: In a radio failure, if all attempts to contact stations fail, with whom is contact attempted last?

90952.text: How is a distress condition defined?
options: A condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance
A condition threatening the safety of a person but not requiring immediate assistance
The aircraft deviating from its planned route
Fuel insufficient to reach the alternate aerodrome

90953.text: What is the basic feature that distinguishes an urgency condition from a distress condition?
options: In urgency, safety is threatened but immediate assistance from outside is not required
Urgency applies only to aircraft on the ground
In urgency the transponder is set to 7700, in distress it is not
An urgency call is made only on 121.5 MHz
The silence rule is applied in an urgency condition

90954.text: What is the radiotelephony distress signal and how many times is it spoken at the start of the message?

90955.text: With which international radio prefix does an urgency call begin?
options: PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN

90956.text: What should a pilot do on hearing an urgency message that is not answered?
options: Acknowledge the message, confirm the situation and relay it to the ground station called

90957.text: Which code is set on the transponder before making the emergency transmission?

90958.text: On which frequency is a distress call made?
options: On the frequency in use at the time; the aircraft stays on it unless advised that another frequency would provide more effective assistance
On the tower frequency of the departure aerodrome
When effective assistance cannot be provided on the frequency in use with the controller

90960.text: Which phrase does the aircraft in distress, or the station controlling it, use to impose silence on the frequency?

90961.text: Which phrase does the pilot use when the distress condition has ended?

90962.text: With which phrase does the controlling station end the imposed silence?

90963.text: Which transponder code is set in the event of unlawful interference (hijack)?

90964.text: Which emergency frequency does the ELT system use for military aviation?

90965.text: Which frequency is used so that the ELT signal can be detected by search and rescue teams?
